problem: Existing zero-shot object navigation relies on language-only goals and ignores pointing gestures, which humans naturally use alongside descriptions to disambiguate a target object in real-world human-agent communication.
motivation: Combining a pointing gesture (direction) with language (name and attributes) allows precise object identification, especially when several instances of a category exist. A task and framework that use both modalities approximate real human-agent interaction more closely.
key_idea: Estimate the pointing direction from human body landmarks, fuse it with depth into a versatile candidate position map (VCPM) that guides exploration, and verify each visited candidate object against the instruction with a large vision-language model.
insight: The abstract suggests the pointing direction acts as a spatial prior that narrows the search, while the LVLM handles attribute-level verification of candidates. Competitive results on Gibson and HM3D without gestures indicate the VCPM-driven exploration and LVLM verification are also effective for standard ObjectNav. No ablations are available, since only the abstract was provided.
method: Pointing gesture estimation: extracts human body landmarks to estimate the pointing direction.
VCPM initialization: fuses the pointing direction with depth images to initialize a versatile candidate position map.
Open-vocabulary detection: detects all potential candidate objects in the environment and projects them onto the VCPM.
VCPM-derived motion policy: drives continuous exploration of the unknown environment and sequential visits to candidates.
LVLM verification: a large vision-language model checks whether each visited candidate satisfies the navigation instruction.

setting.backbone: open-vocabulary detector + large vision-language model (specific models not given in the abstract; training-free)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (depth used for the VCPM); a human pointing image for gesture estimation
setting.action_space: not specified in the abstract (motion policy derived from the VCPM)
setting.simulator: Habitat (Gibson and HM3D datasets); the simulator is not named in the abstract

results: The abstract states that LGNav performs strongly on the new LG-ZSON task. Even without pointing gestures, it achieves competitive results on the Gibson and HM3D ObjectNav benchmarks, outperforming a range of strong baselines. No specific numbers are available.
limitations: Only the abstract was available, so quantitative results and ablations could not be verified.
Depends on reliable human pose and pointing estimation, and on LVLM verification quality.
